transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-02 14:00 PDT
Duration: 49 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Brooks (Redwood SE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood Solutions), Aisha Rahman (IvoryGrid CTO), Tom Ellis (IvoryGrid Platform), Priya Singh (IvoryGrid Security), Ben Cho (IvoryGrid ML)

---
[00:00] Maya: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. Quick audio check?
[00:08] Aisha: Audio's good, thanks. We got the invite, excited to see the console stuff.
[00:12] Maya: Great. Today we'll walk through per-route visibility and cost triage in the Redwood Console. Liam will take most of the demo and Diego will chime in on the sandbox setup.
[00:23] Liam: Hi all, yep, I'll start with where routes surface in the usage view. A quick note, transcription might flip some product terms — I might say K V cash instead of KV cache, ignore that.
[00:33] [screen share starts]
[00:35] Liam: Alright I'm on the demo tenant — first screen is usage overview. You can see total tokens, request counts, and an initial cost estimate. For IvoryGrid we'd map every internal endpoint to a route: aggregator-inference, user-chat, rerank-service, etc.
[01:05] Tom: Quick Q, how granular is the attribution? Do you break down token-level cost per route and per model?
[01:12] Liam: Yes, it's per-token attribution by default. We tag requests by route id and model variant — the console shows token counts, effective gpus seconds, and a cost breakdown column. Keep in mind cost is an estimate based on configured model pricing and the quantization profile.
[01:30] Ben: Does Redwood account for batching differences? We batch heavily and sometimes throughput patterns change cost per token.
[01:36] Liam: Good point. We surface observed batching efficiency metrics — average batch size, tokens per batch, and an efficiency score. Then Optimize recommendations will flag small-batch routes and recommend batching windows or async workers.
[01:56] Priya: Security-wise, how do logs work? We need audit logs, SSO, and KMS integration for keys.
[02:04] Diego: We support SAML SSO and fine-grained RBAC. For key management we integrate with customer KMS/HSM for private deployments; hosted tenants can use Redwood KMS but we also offer BYOK via HSM connectors. We'll share the SOC2 packet after the call.
[02:25] [00:02:30] Maya: I'll drop that SOC2 link in the follow up.
[02:31] [03:00] Liam: Back to routes — here's a per-route timeline. Notice the spike on "rerank-service" early last Tuesday. You can click the spike and drill into request level: prompt lengths, model version, and tokens consumed.
[03:25] [03:30] Ben: I see a lot of long-context calls. Is there a way to automatically identify expensive prefixes to cache?
[03:36] Liam: Yes, do you use prefix caching? We support automatic prefix/KV caching. The console will suggest prefixes with high repetition and show estimated savings if enabled.
[03:50] Tom: We're also worried about tail latency when batching. Can Redwood route low-latency traffic to dedicated capacity and batch background work?
[03:58] Liam: Exactly — routing policies let you assign priority: latency-critical to dedicated nodes, and batch processing to cheaper shared pools. We showed fallback rules: if dedicated is saturated, requests can go to a cheaper variant with lower context length.
[04:18] Priya: For on-prem or VPC customers, how does telemetry get exported? We can't send PII out of region.
[04:26] Diego: For Private deployments, telemetry is stored in your VPC — we provide a private control plane and you can ship metrics to your internal prometheus or S3. Audit logs remain customer-managed.
[04:40] [05:00] Liam: Now cost breakdown — here's the cost ribbon per route. The console decomposes spend into model compute, memory (kv cache warming), and infra overhead. If you click "rerank-service" you can see tokens per call and cost per token by model.
[05:28] Aisha: Can we get an automated alert when a route exceeds an expected spend baseline?
[05:33] Liam: Yes, alerts are first-class. You can set soft and hard thresholds per route; we also have anomaly detection that suggests routes with atypical spend velocity.
[05:45] Ben: Will that detect a mis-routed test job that suddenly floods prod? That's what happened last month.
[05:51] Liam: The velocity alert is designed for that — high token burn for a short window triggers an incident channel. You can configure webhooks to Slack/PagerDuty.
[06:06] [06:10] Maya: Aisha, can you share what your current spend profile looks like roughly? That helps us tune the demo.
[06:13] Aisha: We're still in early staging but run about 800k tokens/day across several endpoints. The user-chat route is the largest, and a small reranker job spikes periodically during batch scoring. We're evaluating whether to move to dedicated for chat.
[06:33] Liam: For 800k tokens, sometimes dedicated is overkill unless you need consistent p95 latency — otherwise Reserved + burst is a middle ground. Optimize will recommend quantization profiles and batch windows that reduce unit cost.
[06:46] Tom: What about model variants? We have a mix of open LLMs and a small proprietary reranker that we host. Can Redwood route to custom model endpoints?
[06:56] Diego: Yes, you can register private model variants. For Private deployments we can onboard your model bundle; for Hosted, you can point to a VPC endpoint if it's in your infra.
[07:10] [07:30] Liam: Now I'm showing a 'cost-forensics' view — you can group by tag, route name, or team. For IvoryGrid you could map routes to product lines or feature flags.
[07:46] Aisha: Mapping to product lines is important for chargeback to business units.
[07:50] Liam: Exactly, and the export feed can push CSVs to billing or your internal finance tools.
[07:58] Ben: Any support for token-level redaction if we send PII?
[08:04] Diego: We have masking/PII filters for telemetry — redaction happens before logs leave the customer VPC in Private mode; for Hosted we offer tokenization options and contract-level controls.
[08:20] [08:30] Maya: Quick break: Priya, is the security team mainly concerned with audit and KMS, or are there network constraints too?
[08:37] Priya: Both. We need proof of encryption at rest and in transit, SSO with SCIM provisioning, and tight network egress control. Also, tenancy model — we prefer dedicated pools for anything that handles sensitive data.
[08:50] Diego: Good, dedicated pools are supported and we provide egress controls via VPC peering and private links.
[08:58] [09:10] Liam: Returning to the console — here's Optimize suggestions for the rerank-service: move quantization to 4-bit for that model, enable prefix caching for the 3 top prompts, and increase batch windows from 20ms to 60ms when latency SLAs allow. The estimated saving shows 28% drop in compute cost.
[09:38] Tom: That estimate—how accurate is it? We need to present reliable numbers to finance.
[09:44] Liam: The console uses observed throughput and kernel-level performance profiles — accuracy is +/- 8% typically, but we'll run a benchmark with your prompts to validate.
[09:52] Ben: Can we schedule that benchmark? We'd like to reproduce the reranker spike pattern.
[09:56] Maya: Absolutely — Liam can run a focused benchmark in the sandbox once you provide sample prompts. We'll also log real-traffic shadows if you want a more realistic test.
[10:08] [10:15] Aisha: Timeline question — if we decide to pilot, how fast can we get sandbox + initial benchmarks running?
[10:20] Diego: Sandbox tenant is typically provisioned in 48-72 hours. Benchmarks take 1-3 days depending on sample size.
[10:27] Priya: Are there legal or procurement gating items for sandbox access?
[10:31] Maya: For sandbox we usually do an MSA + data handling agreement; we'll share a minimal pilot addendum that limits exposure.
[10:39] [11:00] Liam: Switching to alerts and runbooks — here's an example incident: route misconfiguration caused 10x token burn; the console shows exact first-failure timestamp, associated deploy id, and affected model. You can attach runbook steps and assign owners.
[11:22] Tom: That's useful. We want automated rollback or throttles if a route exceeds budget.
[11:29] Liam: We support policy-based throttles: soft stop, hard stop, or degrade to cheaper model. Rollback integration is possible with your CI if you surface deploy ids.
[11:40] Ben: Any client-side SDK hooks to surface route metadata?
[11:44] Liam: Yes SDKs accept route metadata headers and trace ids, which feed into console grouping.
[11:50] [12:10] Maya: Quick interlude — Diego will summarize private deployment options in chat.
[12:15] Diego: Private options: VPC-managed control plane, air-gapped on-prem package, or hybrid where control plane is redwood-hosted and data plane sits in your cloud. All support KMS and audit logging.
[12:33] Priya: For the hybrid model, who owns the logs?
[12:36] Diego: Customer-owned — logs are pushed to your storage account, only aggregates optionally sent to Redwood for product features.
[12:45] [13:00] Liam: Back to cost triage — here's a feature called "Spend Rewind" which will rewind a route's usage back in time to show where cost changed relative to deploys, prompt changes, or model switches. It helped a customer find a prompt template change that doubled tokens.
[13:21] Aisha: That would have helped us last quarter.
[13:25] Ben: Does Spend Rewind keep raw prompts in logs? We have strict retention policies.
[13:30] Diego: Raw prompts retention is configurable; you can store hashes only and keep redacted versions.
[13:40] [14:00] Liam: Now walking through a demo drill: clicking an anomalous spend brightline and drilling to the top contributing requests. You can export the sample requests for offline forensics.
[14:20] Tom: Could that trigger a security review automatically if certain keywords appear?
[14:25] Diego: Yes, we support rule-based content scanners that optionally raise flags to Security.
[14:32] [15:00] Maya: Let's talk pricing shapes — Maya: for the pilot we typically offer a time boxed reserved capacity discount and usage credits against the sandbox.
[15:12] Aisha: We're cost-sensitive but need reliable p95 for chat. What pricing mix do customers usually choose?
[15:18] Maya: Mid-market often picks reserved + burst for chat, plus Shared for background jobs. Larger customers choose Dedicated for critical services. We'll draft a few scenarios in the spreadsheet I'll send.
[15:34] Ben: Any hidden costs like egress or monitoring?
[15:38] Diego: Egress is standard cloud egress; observability retention beyond default may be an add-on. We'll highlight all components in the pricing sheet.
[15:54] [16:30] Liam: Moving on — here's a per-team dashboard that shows spend per feature flag and lets you tag deploys with ticket ids. That helps align engineering and finance.
[16:46] Tom: Nice. That tagging would simplify our chargeback.
[16:50] [17:10] Priya: On compliance, can Redwood do a security workshop? We sometimes need an on-site or deep remote review.
[17:16] Maya: Yes, our security team can run a SOC2 onboarding workshop. We'll include that in the RT.
[17:25] [18:00] Liam: I'm now showing Optimize's "what-if" toggles — slide model quantization, batch size, and routing rules to see projected cost and effect on p95 latency. Here, toggling 8->4-bit shows compute cut but small p95 regression.
[18:28] Ben: Can we pin SLAs per route? E.g., chat p95 120ms.
[18:33] Liam: You can set SLOs per route and get alerts when SLOs slip. Routing policies can ensure p95 targets by moving traffic to a dedicated pool.
[18:45] Aisha: How do you measure p95? Is that end-to-end or server-side?
[18:50] Liam: We report both: client-observed p95 (end-to-end) and server-side p95. For hosted, end-to-end includes network transit. For private, you can inject synthetic probes.
[19:05] [19:30] Maya: We're at 20 minutes now — do you want us to focus next on the benchmark and sandbox provisioning?
[19:36] Aisha: Yes, that's key.
[19:40] Liam: To run a benchmark we'll need 3-5 representative prompts, expected QPS, and any percentile latency targets. We'll simulate your peak profile and produce a comparative report.
[19:56] Ben: We'll extract 50 sample prompts from our reranker logs and send them.
[20:00] Maya: Great — add that to the action items.
[20:06] [20:30] Priya: One last security question: is the private control plane audited as part of your SOC2?
[20:35] Diego: Yes, private deployments are covered; for air-gapped installs we provide an attestation package.
[20:44] [21:15] Liam: Quick demo finish — I exported a sample cost-forensics CSV and a recommended Optimize plan for rerank-service. It includes estimated saving, latency impact, and a rollout plan: canary at 5%, 25%, 100% with fast rollback.
[21:36] Aisha: That rollback path is nice.
[21:40] Tom: What about long-term model rollout management — can we pin variants to routes?
[21:46] Liam: Yes, model pinning and gradual rollouts are built-in, with automatic fallback to previous version if quality or latency regressions occur.
[21:58] [22:30] Maya: Ok, time to recap and firm next steps.
[22:34] Maya: Action items: Maya will send the pilot pricing spreadsheet and SOC2 link; Liam will provision the sandbox and run benchmark once prompts are provided; Priya will send compliance checklist; IvoryGrid will provide sample prompts and an expected traffic profile.
[22:57] Aisha: Sounds good. Expected decision timeline? We're aiming for a pilot in July if all checks out.
[23:05] Maya: That works.
[23:10] [23:30] Ben: Minor note, we may want a short SE-led deep dive on latency kernels for our infra team.
[23:36] Liam: Happy to do a deep dive — Diego can join for private deployment details.
[23:42] [24:00] Maya: Okay, we'll follow up with calendar invites for the benchmark kickoff and deeper SE session. Thanks everyone for the time.
[24:10] Aisha: Thanks, bye.
[24:15] Priya: Bye.
---
Notes on transcript: occasional speaker labels simplified, some product terms may be mistranscribed (eg K V cash / KV cache). Exported artifacts referenced: pilot-pricing.xlsx, SOC2-package.pdf, sandbox-tenant-invite, benchmark-plan.md
